q-48844:
Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)-f(x){g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

At the point where $x=0$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})|}_{x=0} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(0)g(0)-f(0){g}^{′}(0)}{{g}^{2}(0)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1-2\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-48960:
Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)-f(x){g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

At the point where $x=3$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})|}_{x=3} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(3)g(3)-f(3){g}^{′}(3)}{(g(3))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-4)\cdot (-1)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{(-1)^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-104453:
Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)+2g(x))={f}^{′}(x)+2{g}^{′}(x).
$$

At the point where $x=-6$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)+2g(x))|}_{x=-6} & ={f}^{′}(-6)+2{g}^{′}(-6) \\  & =5+2(-2) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-105495:
The product rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(uv)=u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2p(x)+q(x)$ and $v=2-p(x).$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}(x) & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(2p(x)+q(x))(-{p}^{′}(x))+(2-p(x))(2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x)) \\  & =-{p}^{′}(x)(2p(x)+q(x))+(2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x))(2-p(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=10,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}(10) & =-{p}^{′}(10)(2p(10)+q(10))+(2{p}^{′}(10)+{q}^{′}(10))(2-p(10)) \\  & =-(-2)(2(-1)+2)+(2(-2)+1)(2-(-1)) \\  & =2(-2+2)-3(2+1) \\  & =0-9 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

q-103289:
Let's plot the graph of $y=tan⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13933873/assets/732955302ca49a41f6c43cf242d7c869e630e88d804c4b56a5beb3b081f2d230.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined everywhere, except where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .$

- Statement II is false. The zeros occur at $x=0,\pm \pi ,\pm 2\pi ,…,$ which can be written as $x=n\pi .$

- Statement III is false. The function takes values on all the real numbers, hence the range is $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

So, the correct answer is "I only".

q-29608:
Let's recall the graph of $y=tan⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13933873/assets/31b430f003171dcc04a8f17402d6035fbbc305c244d3676bbf5da83fa447bd50.png)

Let's examine each statement.

- Statement I is false. The function $y=tan⁡x$ has asymptotes at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n.$

- Statement II is true. The function has period $\pi .$ So, $tan⁡(x+2n\pi )=tan⁡(x+n\pi +n\pi )=tan⁡(x+n\pi )=tan⁡(x).$

- Statement III is false. The range of $y=tan⁡x$ is $(-\infty ,+\infty ).$

q-70998:
The period of $y=tan⁡x$ is $\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
tan⁡x=tan⁡(x+n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=5$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}tan⁡x=tan⁡(x+5\cdot \pi )=tan⁡(x+5\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $tan⁡x=3,$ we get that $tan⁡(x+5\pi )=3.$

Finally, then

$$
tan⁡(x+5\pi )+2=(3)+2=5.
$$

q-103312:
The period of $y=tan⁡x$ is $\pi .$ Therefore, for any integer $n,$ we have

$$
tan⁡x=tan⁡(x+n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=-9$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}tan⁡x=tan⁡(x+(-9)\cdot \pi )=tan⁡(x-9\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $tan⁡x=16,$ we get that $tan⁡(x-9\pi )=16.$ Therefore

$$
\frac{3}{4}tan⁡(x-9\pi )=\frac{3}{4}(16)=12.
$$

q-136639:

$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}tan⁡(-a) & =-tan⁡a \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}

q-67703:
From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,3}f(x)=9.$ 

Applying the root rule, we get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,3}\frac{\sqrt{25-f(x)}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to \,3}(25-f(x))} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{25-9} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{2} \\  & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-64677:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-{210}^{∘}$ by *adding* integer multiples of ${360}^{∘}$ until we get an angle that lies in the range $[{0}^{∘},{360}^{∘}).$

- $-{210}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={150}^{∘}\,✓$

So the angle ${150}^{∘}$ is coterminal with $-{210}^{∘}.$ Let's draw this coterminal angle in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13933898/assets/788edaa48306f8370f9780cdeda956a85c34b76bd6ec5a028d9d38d425cbc5b9.png)

We see that ${150}^{∘}$ lies in quadrant II. Therefore, $-{210}^{∘}$ also lies in this quadrant.

q-31991:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that our expression can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
{x}^{4}-{y}^{6}={({x}^{2})}^{2}-{({y}^{3})}^{2}
$$

Finally, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
{({x}^{2})}^{2}-{({y}^{3})}^{2}=({x}^{2}+{y}^{3})({x}^{2}-{y}^{3})
$$

q-113303:
In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $g(2-h)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $g:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2-h}-\frac{3}{g(2-h)} & = \\ \frac{g}{g}\cdot \frac{5}{2-h}-\frac{3}{g(2-h)} & = \\ \frac{5g}{g(2-h)}-\frac{3}{g(2-h)} & = \\ \frac{5g-3}{g(2-h)} & \end{aligned}
$$

q-86327:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13933898/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{4}$ corresponds to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $cos⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

q-122083:
In order to find the total number of choices, we can use the **rule of sum**:

$$
5+7+3=15
$$

Therefore, there are $15$ choices of attractions.
